newsitem.title: UK: UK veterans win backing for Gulf War compensation.
newsitem.headline: UK veterans win backing for Gulf War compensation.

text.p: Britain's veterans won a victory in their campaign for compensation for so-called Gulf War syndrome on Thursday when an all-party committee of MPs recommended that some of them receive ex gratia payments.

The Defence Committee's report on the issue was a minor embarrassment for the ruling Conservatives, facing an election on May 1, as it criticised two ministers for having failed to recognise the scale of the problem.

Scores of Britons who served in the 1991 Gulf War campaign following Iraq's invasion of Kuwait have complained of debilitating illness, which they believe was caused by exposure to organophosphate pesticides.

Defence minister Nicholas Soames only agreed in September, following two years of parliamentary questions on the subject, that dangerous organophosphate (OP) chemicals were widely used to protect British troops from disease in the war.

"For those Gulf veterans who can establish that they were exposed to OP pesticides and that there is no other explanation for current illness, we believe that there is a strong case for ex gratia compensation payments," the committee report said.
"We recommend that the government makes such payments."
The committee went on to urge "a thorough re-examination of the system of compensation for service personnel injured while on duty for this country".
Ministers said in reply to parliamentary questions from 1994 onwards that the pesticides were used on only a very small scale to stop the spread of disease among British troops.
Last year, however, they said they had discovered use had been much more widespread than previously believed.
The committee said it would have hoped that Soames and Earl Howe, junior ministers at the Ministry of Defence (MoD), would have been more active in querying the advice they were given.
"We would not wish to underestimate the volume of work that passes across a minister's desk...nor the wide range of subjects with which he has to deal," the report said.

"Nevertheless both Mr Soames and Earl Howe had dealt with the subject of OP poisoning (suffered by farmers dipping sheep) as agriculture ministers before moving to MoD, and, notwithstanding the advantages of hindsight, this is a case where ministerial experience and intuition might have helped."
"We are surprised that ministers were not more pro-active and inquisitive."
